sn35.133:1.2: It is unusual, if not unique, to see a female brahmin with a student. Below, she is referred to as the “tutor’s wife” (_ācariyabhariyā_); compare Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10, where a tutor’s wife (_ācāryajāyā_) discusses the education of the pupil with her husband. Verahaccāni is not an attested clan name, and Sanskrit _vairahatya_ means “manslaughter”. Given that her husband is rather mysteriously absent, perhaps _verahaccāni_ is a term for brahmin ladies whose husbands were murdered. Compare _nirvīrā_, a woman whose husband and children are dead. If so, it would seem that she did not merely survive her husband’s passing, but stepped into his role as teacher.
sn35.133:2.7: She adopts these as signifiers of status. Perhaps as a woman she felt the need to assert her status. Nonetheless, the rules of training forbid monastics from teaching someone wearing slippers ([pli-tv-bu-vb-sk61]()), sitting on a high seat ([pli-tv-bu-vb-sk69]()), or with head covered ([pli-tv-bu-vb-sk67]()).
